(p-633)Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah (The Overwhelming)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ [The particle] *hal*, in the sense of *qad* (indeed, already),

﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾, the calamity that covers people with its hardships and clothes them with its terrors, meaning the Resurrection. It was also said: the Fire, from His saying: ﴿and the Fire covers their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 2:

﴿Faces﴾ meaning: the faces of the disbelievers. He specified the face because grief and joy, when they take firm hold of a person, leave their mark upon the face.

﴿On that Day﴾, the Day when it (the Overwhelming Event) envelops them.

﴿Humbled﴾, abased, because of the disgrace and humiliation that befall their owners.

﴿Working, toiling﴾: it labours in the Fire at a labour that wearies it, namely dragging the chains and shackles, its wading through the Fire as camels wade through mud, its climbing ceaselessly up a ascent of fire, and its descending down slopes of it. It is also said: it worked evil deeds in the world and took pleasure in them and luxuriated in them, so in the Hereafter it is in toil from them. It is also said: they are the people of the monasteries, and the meaning is that they were humble before God, and they worked, and toiled in their deeds, through constant fasting and tiresome night prayer.
﴿Burning in a scorching fire.﴾ It enters a fire that has been heated for long periods, so no heat is equal to its heat. "تُصْلى" (read as *tuslā*), Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr [read it this way]. (p-٦٣٤)

﴿They will be given drink from a spring, intensely hot﴾: from a spring of water whose heat has reached its extreme. The feminine forms in these attributes and verbs refer back to "faces" (wujuh), and what is meant is their possessors (ashabuha), as is shown by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 6:

﴿There is no food for them except from ḍarī⁶ (a thorny plant).﴾ It is a plant called "al-shibriq" (a kind of wild plant). When it dries, it becomes ḍarī⁶, and it is a deadly poison. The punishments are of various kinds, and those who are punished are of various levels. Among them are those who eat the zaqqum (the tree of Hell), among them are those who eat the ghislin (the pus and filth of the damned), and among them are those who eat the ḍarī⁶. Thus there is no contradiction between this verse and His words: ﴿And no food except from ghislin﴾ [al-Haqqah: 36].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 7:

﴿Neither nourishes⁠﴾, genitive in its position, because it is an attribute of "ḍarī" (a bitter, thorny plant),

﴿nor does it satisfy hunger﴾, meaning: the two benefits of food are absent from it, and they are: removing hunger, and producing fatness in the body.

﴿Faces on that Day﴾. Then he described the faces of the believers, and he did not say "وَوُجُوهٌ" (wa-wujūhun, "and faces"), because the first statement had become long and had come to an end.

﴿Joyful﴾: enjoying a life of ease and comfort.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 9:

﴿Pleased with their striving﴾: they are pleased with their deeds and their obedience, when they see what their striving has brought them of honour and reward.
﴿In a lofty garden﴾, lofty in terms of place, or in terms of rank.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 11:

﴿You will not hear﴾ O addressee, or the faces (are the subject),

﴿therein any idle talk﴾, i.e., vain speech, or a word of idle talk, or a soul that engages in idle talk. The people of Paradise speak only with wisdom and with praise of God for the lasting bliss with which He has provided them. "Not heard therein is any idle talk" (lā yusma'u fīhā lāghiyatun) is the reading of Makki and Abu 'Amr; and "You will not hear therein any idle talk" (lā tusma'u fīhā lāghiyatan) is the reading of Nafi'.
﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾, i.e., many springs, like His saying: ﴿a soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 13:

﴿In it are couches⁠﴾, the plural of "sarir" (couch),

﴿raised high⁠﴾, either from loftiness of rank or from height, so that the believer, by sitting upon it, may behold all the dominion and bliss that his Lord has bestowed upon him.

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿وَأكْوابٌ﴾ = "And cups"; ﴿مَوْضُوعَةٌ﴾ = "placed".

**Translation:**

﴿And cups﴾, the plural of "kūb" (a cup with no handle), which is a vessel for drinking; and it is said: a vessel with no handle. (p-635) ﴿placed﴾ before them, so that they may delight in them by looking at them; or they are placed on the edges of the springs, prepared for drinking.

"And cushions" (نَمارِقُ), meaning pillows (وسائد),

"arranged in rows" (مَصْفُوفَةٌ), meaning placed side by side, some beside others; backrests and mattresses (مَسانِدُ ومَطارِحُ). Wherever he wishes to sit, he sits on one and leans back against another.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 88, verse 16:

﴿And carpets (zarabi)﴾, broad, splendid spreads, the plural of "zirbiyyah" (a rich cushion or carpet),

﴿spread out (mabthuthah)﴾, laid out, or scattered throughout the assemblies. When Allah (Exalted) revealed these verses describing Paradise, and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained that the height of the couch would be a hundred farsakh, and that the cups set out there would not enter into the reckoning of creation because of their multitude, and that the length of the cushions was such-and-such, and the breadth of the carpets was such-and-such, the disbelievers denied it and said: "How can one ascend this couch?! And how can the cups be so numerous, and the cushions so long, and the carpets spread out so widely? We have never witnessed such things in this world?!" Then Allah (Exalted) said:

Will they not look at the camels, how they were created? [They are] tall, then they kneel down so that they may be ridden and loaded upon, then they stand up. Likewise the couch (sarir): it lowers itself for the believer, just as the camel lowers itself.

﴿And at the sky, how it is raised﴾: raised to a far-reaching height, without supports and without pillars. Then its stars are so numerous in this abundance that they do not enter into the reckoning of creation; so likewise [are] the cups.

And at the mountains, how they have been set up. (Qur'an 88:19)

"How they have been set up": a firm setting, so they are fixed and do not lean, despite their height. Likewise the cushions.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 88, verse 20:

﴿And at the earth, how it has been spread out?﴾ It is spread out (*sataḥan*) by being leveled and made smooth (*tamhīd* and *tawṭi'a*), so it is all one continuous expanse (*bisāṭ wāḥid*), stretching from horizon to horizon, just as the carpets (*al-zarābī*, i.e., cushions and rugs) are spread out. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Do they not look at these created things that bear witness to the power of the Creator, so that they do not deny His ability to resurrect (*al-ba'th*), and so that they hear the warning of the Messenger, believe in him, and prepare for their meeting with Him?" The singling out of these four (the camel, the sky, the mountains, and the earth) is because this is an address to the Arabs and an exhortation for them to reason from evidence. A person only reasons from what he sees often, and the Arabs lived in the desert (*al-bawādī*), where their looking was directed at the sky, the earth, and the mountains, and the camel was the most precious of their property. They used it more than they used the other animals, and because it combines all the desired benefits from an animal: offspring, milk, carrying loads, riding, and food, unlike others. Also, its creation is more wondrous than others, for He subjected it to be obedient to whoever leads it by its reins. It does not overpower the weak, nor does it resist the young. He created it with long necks so that it can bear heavy burdens, and made it such that it kneels so that it can be loaded easily and without difficulty, then rises with what it has carried and carries it to distant lands (*al-bilād al-shāḥiṭa*). He made it patient in enduring thirst, to the extent that its thirst may last ten days or more, and He made it graze on every plant that grows in the wilderness (*al-barārī*), which the other beasts do not graze.

﴿So remind﴾: remind them with the proofs so that they may reflect upon them.

﴿You are only a reminder﴾: there is nothing incumbent upon you except conveying (the message).

"You are not over them a controller" — meaning, not one who has power over them (bi-mutasallit), like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a tyrant﴾ [Qaf: 45]. "Bi-musaytir" (with sin, read with sād), "Madani, Basri, ʿAli and ʿAsim" (read it as such, with the letter sād in place of sīn).

The exception here is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: you are not responsible for them; but whoever among them turns away and disbelieves in God, then God has the authority over him and the power to subdue him, so He will punish him with the greatest punishment, which is the punishment of Hell. It is also said that it is an exception from His saying "so remind" (fa-dhakkir), meaning: remind, except for the one whose hope of his faith you have given up, who turns away, and so deserves the greatest punishment. And what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD).

Indeed, to Us is their return (﴿إنَّ إلَيْنا إيابَهُمْ﴾), i.e., their coming back (رُجُوعَهُمْ). The benefit of fronting the adverbial phrase (ظرف, al-zarf) is to emphasize the severity of the threat, and that their return is to none but the Almighty (الجَبّار), the One Able to exact retribution.

Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning.** ﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾: We will call them to account for their deeds, and We will recompense them for them with the recompense of their like. The word "ʿalā" (upon) is for emphasizing the threat, not for obligation, since nothing is obligatory upon God.
